title: Neuroscience, the Natural Environment, and Building Design.
research_question: How do human nature, neurological processes, and evolutionary adaptations influence human response to the built environment, and how can biophilic design reconnect humans to their surroundings for enhanced wellbeing?

participants.description: Not applicable, theoretical/review paper synthesizing existing research.

findings.antecedent: Designs which connect humans to the lived experience (biophilic design)
findings.consequent: Overall sense of wellbeing, positive and therapeutic physiological consequences
findings.mechanism: Not explicitly stated for this specific finding, but the paper proposes informational connectivity and neurological nourishment.
findings.quote: Empirical evidence confirms that designs which connect humans to the lived experience enhance our overall sense of wellbeing, with positive and therapeutic consequences on physiology.

findings.antecedent: Architectural forms and surfaces
findings.mechanism: Connection established via information exchange, neurological mechanism reacts to information field.
findings.quote: We engage emotionally with the built environment through architectural forms and surfaces.

findings.antecedent: Environmental information field (from built environment)
findings.mechanism: Our neurological mechanism reacts to the information field (the transmission component), while inducing a reaction in the state of our body (the physiological component).
findings.quote: Our neurological mechanism reacts to the information field (the transmission component), while inducing a reaction in the state of our body (the physiological component).

findings.antecedent: Intrinsic qualities of natural and built environments (e.g., organized complexity, fractal patterns)
findings.mechanism: Works through the sense of wellbeing established and maintained.
findings.quote: Both natural and built environments possess intrinsic qualities that enable such a strong connection, and which in turn can be healing.

findings.antecedent: Certain types of environmental information (e.g., organized complexity, fractals)
findings.consequent: Activation of brain's pleasure centers, reduction of pain
findings.mechanism: Humans have an innate hunger for certain types of information.
findings.quote: Humans have an innate hunger for certain types of information: the circuits for this have been associated with the brain's pleasure centers, which also control the reduction of pain

findings.antecedent: Fractal qualities in our environment (ordered details arranged in a nested scaling hierarchy)
findings.quote: A growing amount of research finds that fractal qualities in our environment (i.e., ordered details arranged in a nested scaling hierarchy) contribute positively to human wellbeing

findings.antecedent: Viewing natural environments (or videos of natural environments)
findings.mechanism: Link between specific types of informational input and pain reduction.
findings.quote: Pain relief in hospital settings is significantly improved by viewing natural (or videos of natural) environments... thus confirming the link between specific types of informational input and pain reduction.

findings.antecedent: Neurologically-nourishing environment
findings.mechanism: It is built into our neural system.
findings.quote: Reaction to a neurologically-nourishing environment is physiological (i.e. emotional) rather than intellectual.

findings.antecedent: Visual complexity of the natural environment (highest levels of organized complexity)
findings.consequent: Positive response from innate information-processing system
findings.mechanism: An innate information-processing system that has evolved along with the rest of our physiology is acutely tuned to visual complexity.
findings.quote: This system is acutely tuned to the visual complexity of the natural environment, specifically to respond positively to the highest levels of organized complexity

findings.antecedent: Geometrical properties of natural/biological forms (beyond fractals)
findings.quote: Additional geometrical properties of natural/biological forms clearly contribute to a positive physiological response in humans

findings.antecedent: Environmental information (presence and organization)
findings.consequent: Positive or negative effect on perceptive system
findings.quote: Not only the presence of information, but especially how that information is organized, produces a positive or negative effect on our perceptive system

findings.antecedent: Structures embodying organized complexity (vs. plain or disorganized complexity)
findings.quote: Human beings connect physiologically and psychologically to structures embodying organized complexity more strongly than to environments that are either too plain, or which present disorganized complexity

findings.antecedent: Flat lawn (single scale, lacking fractal complexity)
findings.consequent: Inability of senses to connect fractally
findings.mechanism: Our senses perceive it as a single scale and are unable to connect to it fractally.
findings.quote: A flat lawn... Our senses perceive it as a single scale and are unable to connect to it fractally.

findings.antecedent: Interacting plants (providing visual complexity)
findings.mechanism: Interacting plants provide visual complexity, which is a source of neurological nourishment.
findings.quote: interacting plants that in turn provide visual complexity, which is a source of neurological nourishment.

findings.antecedent: Industrial building (even with grafted biological components)
findings.consequent: Neurological disconnection, hostility to human sensibilities
findings.mechanism: The natural aspect of an industrial building-plus-garden is simply a biological component grafted onto an armature that is fundamentally hostile to human sensibilities.
findings.quote: The natural aspect of an industrial building-plus-garden is simply a biological component grafted onto an armature that is fundamentally hostile to human sensibilities. It still triggers an underlying neurological disconnection on a basic level.

findings.antecedent: Traditional ornamentation, color, articulated surfaces, and the shape of interior space
findings.quote: Traditional ornamentation, color, articulated surfaces, and the shape of interior space helped to achieve informational connectivity.

findings.antecedent: Ornamentation (distilling geometrical connective rules)
findings.mechanism: Ornamentation in its deepest expressions is a distillation of geometrical connective rules that trigger our neurophysiology directly.
findings.quote: ornamentation in its deepest expressions is far more than that: it is a distillation of geometrical connective rules that trigger our neurophysiology directly.

findings.antecedent: Dominant 20th-century architectural ideology (lacking geometrical connective rules)
findings.quote: These qualities are emphatically not present in the dominant architectural ideology of the twentieth century.

findings.antecedent: Underlying geometrical complexity of living structure (in organisms, artifacts, buildings)
findings.quote: the underlying geometrical complexity of living structure is what nourishes humans. This geometry could be equally expressed in biological organisms as in artifacts and buildings: the difference is merely one of degree

findings.antecedent: Historic sacred sites, buildings, and artifacts
findings.quote: the most intense connection is achieved in historic sacred sites, buildings, and artifacts.

findings.antecedent: Automated, disconnected population (conditioned against biological nature)
findings.consequent: Insensitivity to healing effects of natural environments
findings.mechanism: Human beings can be psychologically conditioned to act against their biological nature.
findings.quote: An automated, disconnected population is insensitive to the healing effects of natural environments.

findings.antecedent: Neurologically non-nourishing built environment
findings.consequent: Negative instinctive reaction, physical anxiety, distress
findings.mechanism: Our response mechanisms still operate automatically.
findings.quote: Therefore, we will instinctively react in a negative manner to a built environment that is neurologically non-nourishing, or which might actually cause physical anxiety and distress.

findings.antecedent: Geometry of the environment (in hospitals)
findings.quote: In hospital design, the geometry of the environment plays a significant role in how long it takes for a patient to be cured.

findings.antecedent: Symmetry, visual connections, ornament, and fine detail on buildings
findings.mechanism: Our perception is built to engage with those features.
findings.quote: Symmetry, visual connections, ornament, and fine detail are necessary on buildings; not for any stylistic reason, but because our perception is built to engage with those features

findings.antecedent: Environment eschewing natural/traditional visual elements (symmetry, detail, etc.)
findings.consequent: Negative physiological consequences, negative mental health, decreased wellbeing
findings.quote: Creating an environment that deliberately eschews these elements... has negative consequences for our physiology, and thus for our mental health and sense of wellbeing

findings.antecedent: Environments devoid of neurologically-nourishing information (colorless, drab, minimalist surfaces/spaces)
findings.consequent: Mimicry of human pathology symptoms (macular degeneration, stroke, etc.)
findings.quote: Environments devoid of neurologically-nourishing information mimic signs of human pathology. For example, colorless, drab, minimalist surfaces and spaces reproduce clinical symptoms of macular degeneration, stroke, cerebral achromatopsia, and visual agnosia

findings.antecedent: Environments devoid of neurologically-nourishing information
findings.consequent: Anxiety, sensation of sensory deprivation/neurophysiologic breakdown
findings.mechanism: They provoke in us a similar sensation as sensory deprivation and neurophysiologic breakdown.
findings.quote: We feel anxious in such environments, because they provoke in us a similar sensation as sensory deprivation and neurophysiologic breakdown.

findings.antecedent: More naturalistic habitats (for zoo animals)
findings.quote: implementing a transformation towards more naturalistic habitats... the animals' psychological and social well-being has been drastically improved.

findings.antecedent: Drab, monotonous, and minimalist environments (for zoo animals)
findings.quote: Zoo animals kept in drab, monotonous, and minimalist environments... exhibited neurotic, aberrant, and antisocial behavior never observed in the wild.

findings.antecedent: Moving to more naturalistic and stimulating habitats (for zoo animals)
findings.consequent: Return to normal, healthier behavior patterns
findings.quote: Moved to more naturalistic and stimulating habitats, the animals returned to more normal, healthier behavior patterns.

findings.antecedent: Environmental complexity and stimulation
findings.consequent: Increased intelligence of a developing animal
findings.quote: complexity and stimulation in the environment can lead to increased intelligence of a developing animal.

findings.antecedent: Information-rich environments (for young rats)
findings.consequent: Increased brain size, improved neural connectivity (up to 20%)
findings.mechanism: Optimizes the cortical physiology responsible for intelligence.
findings.quote: Incontrovertible results are obtained with young rats raised in information-rich environments, whose brains increase in size, and can improve their neural connectivity by up to 20%

findings.antecedent: Enriched environments (for rats)
findings.consequent: Improved performance in intelligence tests (solving complex maze problems), improved training
findings.quote: Those rats raised in enriched environments are then observed to do much better in intelligence tests (such as solving complex maze problems) and training.

findings.antecedent: Room with hierarchical subdivisions and natural detail (vs. plain room)
findings.quote: In a clinical comparison of two distinct environments, one a plain room, and the other with wooden beams added to create hierarchical scaling, the subjects did not express any preference. Yet the physiological monitors recorded a marked response in favor of the room with hierarchical subdivisions and natural detail

findings.antecedent: Environmental features
findings.quote: physiological effects of the environment cannot always be consciously recognized.

findings.antecedent: Sensory input
findings.quote: Emotional learning is the result of sensory input, but remains subconscious (i.e. stored in nondeclarative memory).

findings.antecedent: Emotionally learned patterns (satisfying internal template)
findings.mechanism: They satisfy an internal template.
findings.quote: Patterns learned emotionally through perception act in the same way as inherited (genetically-based) responses. The reason they evoke a positive emotion to begin with, is because they satisfy an internal template.

findings.antecedent: Robots mimicking human behaviors (eye/head movement, facial expressions, speech, movement)
findings.consequent: Perceived "aliveness", involuntary engagement, disappointment/shock when non-human
findings.mechanism: The observer interacts through patterns of a very specific type of complexity that is characteristic of living, and specifically human, beings.
findings.quote: They have an “aliveness” to them that is most unusual in inanimate objects. People respond involuntarily in a way that engages the robots, and seem disappointed or shocked when these robots occasionally act in a non-human manner

findings.antecedent: Increasing complexity of interaction (aligned with neurophysiology and sensory apparatus)
findings.quote: Increasing the complexity of interaction in a definite direction (defined precisely by what our neurophysiology and sensory apparatus are built to detect) eventually leads to higher degrees of human connectivity.

findings.antecedent: Contact with domestic animals
findings.mechanism: Information exchange, which is richly complex and pattern-based.
findings.quote: people have benefited from (and documented) the positive emotional and health effects of contact with domestic animals.

findings.antecedent: Spiritual moments
findings.consequent: Feeling most alive, deep connection to environment and universe
findings.quote: Human beings feel most alive in their spiritual moments. In such instances, we feel connected to our environment, in a deep sense belonging to it and to the universe.

findings.antecedent: Sacred spaces (in traditional cultures)
findings.consequent: Unusually high degree of human connection
findings.quote: All traditional cultures have built sacred spaces in which one experiences an unusually high degree of connection.

findings.antecedent: Sacred spaces
findings.mechanism: The same process that underlies the biophilic phenomenon, via informational fields.
findings.quote: Sacred spaces are nourishing to whoever occupies them.

findings.antecedent: Minimalist churches (without natural elements, figurative art, or ornament)
findings.consequent: Failure to engage the user in any positive way
findings.quote: Without natural elements, figurative art, or ornament, they fail to engage the user in any positive way.

findings.antecedent: Empty informational field (minimalist design)
findings.quote: Their empty informational field only communicates sensory deprivation, provoking physiological unease.

findings.antecedent: Architecture driven by images and surface effects (supplanting human desires and sensibilities)
findings.consequent: Ill-fitting, over-exaggerated, and idiosyncratic formal architectural schemes (for humans)
findings.quote: When images and surface effects supplant everyday human desires and sensibilities in the name of artistic endeavor, humans are left to live out their lives in a series of ill-fitting, over-exaggerated, and often idiosyncratic formal architectural schemes.

findings.antecedent: Natural and traditional built environments (rich in informational content)
findings.quote: the natural and traditional built environments rich in informational content make a place more intrinsically human.

findings.antecedent: Lack of coherent design of intermediate and larger scales (lacking proper scaling hierarchy)
findings.quote: the intermediate and larger scales have not been designed coherently in recent decades, so the fractal connective effect (which emerges only with the proper scaling hierarchy) is lost.

findings.antecedent: Density of subsymmetries, intensity of interaction across distinct scales
findings.quote: The density of subsymmetries, and their intensity of interaction inside a particular scale and across distinct scales, is what leads to visual coherence.

findings.antecedent: Repeated identical components/modules
findings.consequent: Inability to achieve emergent informational higher scale
findings.quote: This emergent phenomenon is impossible to achieve with repeated identical components or modules.

findings.antecedent: Construction hiding natural materials (e.g., sheetrock over wood)
findings.consequent: Inability to connect to abstracted geometry, loss of informational content
findings.mechanism: Hides materials with greatest informational content, presenting abstracted geometry.
findings.quote: This type of construction hides the materials with the greatest informational content, presenting instead an abstracted geometry to which we cannot connect.

findings.antecedent: Rough stone and brick surfaces (hostile to touch)
findings.quote: their surface is hostile to the touch, thus they should be located out of immediate reach.

findings.antecedent: "Industrial look"
findings.quote: there is no connective value in an “industrial look”.

findings.antecedent: 19th-Century modular ornamental panels (high encoded information)
findings.quote: this form of architectural expression contains a high degree of encoded information and is thus very useful for establishing human wellbeing.

findings.antecedent: Natural materials from older buildings
findings.consequent: High informational load (difficult to duplicate in new materials without high cost)
findings.quote: Their informational load cannot be duplicated in new materials without incurring a considerably higher cost.

findings.antecedent: Material logic of natural materials
findings.quote: The material logic of these natural materials provides yet another level of neurological connectivity.

findings.antecedent: Unfinished concrete (lacking ordered microstructure)
findings.quote: Unfinished concrete has an informationally frustrating surface because it lacks ordered microstructure.

findings.antecedent: Concrete formed with wooden planks (wood grain impression, but lacking fractal scaling into microstructure)
findings.consequent: Lack of visual coherence, unnatural appearance
findings.quote: using wooden planks to form the concrete does leave a wood grain impression, but this does not produce a visually-coherent surface because it does not have the correct fractal scaling into microstructure, and at best seems unnatural.

findings.antecedent: Individual input from craftsmen (in construction)
findings.quote: By allowing individual input in this manner, we imbue the architecture with a life outside the frozen expression typically conceived on the drawing board.

findings.antecedent: Repeated identical components/standardized modules
findings.quote: The same degree of life would be impossible to achieve with repeated identical components such as the standardized modules now available for construction.

findings.antecedent: Mathematical coherence (from fractal geometry)
findings.quote: The mathematical coherence established through the effective application of fractal geometry elicits the neurological engagement required for a sense of wellbeing.

findings.antecedent: Complex piece of nature (1-2 meters in size)
findings.quote: Intensify a fairly intimate scale: a complex piece of nature existing on the scale of a human being (1-2 meters in size) can make a substantial difference to our biophilic connection.

findings.antecedent: Complex geometry of native wild plants
findings.quote: Native plants growing wild define a particular complex geometry, and this is the geometry that can best serve to keep us healthy and make us well.

findings.antecedent: Suburban space (vast expanses of flat lawn and asphalt)
findings.quote: The worst disaster is suburban space, in which vast expanses of flat lawn and asphalt define a psychologically-hostile environment for the pedestrian.

mechanisms: Neurological mechanisms reacting to information fields
Innate hunger for certain types of information, associated with brain's pleasure centers and pain reduction
Organized information and its structure affecting perceptive system
Genetic factors underlying connection to biological forms and healing effects
Evolution of innate information-processing system tuned to visual complexity
Hierarchical connections and organized details connecting humans to living structure
Ornamentation as distillation of geometrical connective rules triggering neurophysiology
Expert knowledge as internalized complex data, providing patterns for unconscious matching
Genetic and learned components of memory/sensory systems working as innate responses
Emotional learning as subconscious, nondeclarative memory satisfying internal templates
Patterns of complexity characteristic of living beings engaging observers
Material logic of natural materials providing neurological connectivity
Mathematical coherence from fractal geometry eliciting neurological engagement
implementation_implications: Incorporate organic life and natural geometry into the built environment.
Bring nature into buildings, use natural materials, allow natural light, and incorporate plants into the structure.
Set buildings within natural environments instead of simply erasing nature.
Support ecosystems and native plant species whenever possible.
Incorporate small ecosystems and rich plant combinations within buildings or courtyards.
Design built geometry to follow the same complexity as natural forms.
Use traditional ornamentation, color, articulated surfaces, and interior space shapes to achieve informational connectivity.
Build intensely connective buildings based on scientific understanding of the natural world's geometry.
Re-orient architecture towards optimizing neurological engagement.
Develop new structural systems that preserve natural materials for visible, touchable surfaces.
Re-use natural materials from older buildings and incorporate architectural salvage materials into new designs.
Use natural unfinished materials and avoid over-controlling construction to uniform modular sizes.
Manipulate concrete with patterns to provide positive sensory feedback.
Give craftsmen freedom for individual expression in the construction process to foster pleasurable feedback.
Utilize high technology and robotic manufacturing to generate varied components that mimic natural variations.
Apply fractal geometry for mathematical coherence and neurological engagement.
Geometrically interweave plant life and natural features with the building fabric.
Abandon rectangular or convex building footprints for more meandering or crenellated boundaries that surround gardens, verandas, and patios.
Intensify complex pieces of nature (1-2 meters in size) to make a substantial difference to biophilic connection.
Resist the conditioned impulse toward "purity" in modernist designs and allow high levels of natural engagement.
Establish and create natural geometry where it is absent, and reinforce it where it already exists.
Make gardens physically accessible and coherently designed for enjoyment.
Break up suburban no-man's-land into well-defined urban spaces crisscrossed by paths.
Focus urban planning away from uniformity, designing many complex natural areas and resisting homogenization of green spaces.
Apply a natural (fractal) distribution of sizes to green spaces in the city (many small, several intermediate, few large).
Ensure each green space has its own internal distribution with complexity and variety.
Architects must be fully engaged from start to finish in the construction process, moving towards the historical model of the Master Builder.
limitations: The paper is a theoretical synthesis and literature review, and does not present new empirical data from the authors' own studies.

paper_metadata.title: Restoration in Urban Spaces
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Despite promising experimental findings, few studies have addressed the potential long-term health benefits of frequent contact with different kinds of urban nature. We examine the cross-sectional relations between two kinds of urban nature (neighborhood vegetation visible from the home, use of public green spaces) and health outcomes (life satisfaction, perceived general health, 2-months hair cortisol levels) in a sample population from Berlin ( N = 32) using a mixed-method approach. Participants whose homes had views of high amounts of diverse kinds of vegetation had significantly lower cortisol levels. Moreover, participants who regularly used a vegetated trail along a canal had significantly lower cortisol levels and reported significantly higher life satisfaction than less frequent users. In addition, vegetated routes or paths played an important role in the restorative activities and daily commutes of participants. We discuss directions for future research and recommend more consideration of greenways in urban development.
